title: Conjecture 1.1 (Guo, Kang and Zwaneveld)
statement_text: For every graph $G$ and every integer $d\geq 0$, we have $\chi(G)=\chi^{d}(G\boxtimes K_{d+1})$.
context_text: Motivated by studying the tightness of Hoffman's spectral bound on the chromatic number and its $d$-defective extension by Bilu, Guo, Kang and Zwaneveld conjectured an exact equality between the ordinary chromatic number of $G$ and the $d$-defective chromatic number of its $(d+1)$-fold clique blowup. The conjecture was also posed as an open problem at the 2025 Graph Theory workshop in Oberwolfach. The easy direction $\chi^{d}(G\boxtimes K_{d+1})\leq\chi(G)$ holds by lifting an optimal proper coloring; the heart of the conjecture is the reverse inequality.
paper_contribution: Disproves the conjecture by constructing graphs $G$ of arbitrarily large chromatic number such that $\chi(G)\geq\frac{30}{29}\chi^{d}(G\boxtimes K_{d+1})$ for infinitely many $d$; on the positive side proves the constant-factor version $\chi^{d}(G\boxtimes K_{d+1})\leq\chi(G)\leq 2\chi^{d}(G\boxtimes K_{d+1})$ for every graph $G$ and $d\geq 0$.

title: Problem 1.4
statement_text: Determine $\sup\left\{\frac{\chi(G)}{\chi^d(G\boxtimes K_{d+1})} : G \text{ is a graph and } d\ge 0\right\}$, i.e. the smallest value of $c$ for which the inequality $\chi(G)\leq c\cdot\chi^{d}(G\boxtimes K_{d+1})$ always holds.
context_text: For an integer $d\ge0$, a colouring of $G$ is $d$-defective if every colour class induces a subgraph of maximum degree at most $d$ (each vertex has at most $d$ neighbours of its own colour), and the $d$-defective chromatic number $\chi^d(G)$ is the minimum number of colours in a $d$-defective colouring. $G\boxtimes K_{d+1}$ is the strong product, i.e. the blowup of $G$ obtained by replacing each vertex by a clique of size $d+1$ and joining all vertices of the cliques of $u$ and $v$ whenever $uv\in E(G)$. Lifting a proper colouring of $G$ gives $\chi^d(G\boxtimes K_{d+1})\le\chi(G)$ always. Guo, Kang and Zwaneveld conjectured that equality $\chi(G)=\chi^d(G\boxtimes K_{d+1})$ always holds (true for $d\le1$, perfect graphs, and $\chi(G)\le4$). The authors disprove it: for every $d\ge2$ there is a graph $G$ with $\chi^d(G\boxtimes K_{d+1})\le k:=2d^3+2d^2+d+3$ but $\chi(G)>k$; for $d=2$ this gives a ratio $\frac{30}{29}$, so the supremum is at least $\frac{30}{29}$. They also prove $\chi(G)\le2\chi^d(G\boxtimes K_d)\le2\chi^d(G\boxtimes K_{d+1})$ for all $G$ and $d\ge1$, so the supremum is at most $2$. By bootstrapping, for all $d\equiv2\pmod 3$ and $k\equiv0\pmod{30}$ there is $G$ with $\chi(G)=k\ge\frac{30}{29}\chi^d(G\boxtimes K_{d+1})$, so assuming $\chi(G)$ or $d$ large does not bring the ratio arbitrarily close to $1$.
